clinicalPearls: GI NETs are broadly grouped by origin into extrapancreatic NETs (historically called carcinoid tumors) and pancreatic NETs; they typically follow a more indolent course than most malignancies but can synthesize peptides, growth factors, and bioactive amines that are ectopically secreted (Harrison 22e p.676).

Tumors are classified by differentiation (well vs poorly differentiated) and grade 1-3, which closely correlates with mitotic count and Ki-67 index: grade 1 is <2 mitoses/10 HPF and Ki-67 <3%, grade 2 is 2-20/10 HPF and 3-20%, grade 3 is >20/10 HPF and >20%; poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas are the most aggressive category (Harrison 22e p.677).

Only about 20% of pancreatic NETs are functional (hormone-secreting); the majority are nonfunctional and present incidentally or with mass-related symptoms such as abdominal pain and weight loss (Harrison 22e p.677).
The most common functional pancreatic NET is insulinoma, followed by glucagonoma and gastrinoma; somatostatinoma, VIPoma, ACTHoma and others are uncommon (Harrison 22e p.677).

Most gastrinomas actually arise in the gastrinoma triangle (bounded by duodenum, pancreas, and confluence of cystic and common bile ducts) rather than the pancreas, and 50-90% of sporadic gastrinomas arise in the duodenum, where they are often small and hard to localize (Harrison 22e p.678).

Glucagonoma classically presents with necrolytic migratory erythema (often intertriginous, waxing and waning), glucose intolerance and weight loss; a hypercoagulable state is reported in up to one-third of patients (Harrison 22e p.679).

Gastric NETs fall into three types: type 1 (chronic atrophic gastritis, most common, generally benign), type 2 (associated with gastrinoma/ZES), and type 3 (sporadic, normal gastrin, potentially far more aggressive) (Harrison 22e p.680).

Small-bowel NETs (most often terminal ileum) arise within the muscularis/submucosa and are notoriously hard to diagnose early; mesenteric fibrosis from serotonin-driven fibroblast proliferation produces a classic calcified spoke-and-wheel mesenteric mass on CT and can cause intermittent obstruction and bowel ischemia (Harrison 22e p.680).

Carcinoid syndrome (flushing, watery diarrhea, right-sided valvular heart disease, mesenteric fibrosis) is most associated with small intestine or appendiceal primaries and usually develops only after hepatic metastases or retroperitoneal lesions allow serotonin and vasoactive substances to enter systemic circulation (Harrison 22e p.681).

More than 90% of NETs express somatostatin receptors, making somatostatin-analogue PET tracers (gallium-68 dotatate, DOTATOC, copper-64 dotatate) highly sensitive for detecting primaries and metastases (Harrison 22e p.681).

Carcinoid heart disease occurs in roughly two-thirds of patients with carcinoid syndrome and is characterized by plaque-like fibrous endocardial thickening classically on the right heart, causing tricuspid regurgitation (nearly universal) plus possible tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary regurgitation, and pulmonary stenosis (Harrison 22e p.683).

A minority of NETs arise within inherited syndromes; MEN 1 (menin gene, 11q13) is the most common, and gastrinoma should prompt a family history and assessment for hyperparathyroidism since up to 25% of ZES patients have MEN 1 (Harrison 22e p.676, 678).
harrison.pathophysiology: GI NETs arise from neuroendocrine cells and contain electron-dense neurosecretory granules holding peptides and bioactive amines that can be ectopically secreted. Sporadic pancreatic NETs most frequently harbor MEN1 mutations (about 44%), with frequent mutations in the DAXX/ATRX chromatin-remodeling complex (about 43%) and mTOR-pathway genes (about 15%); recurrent mutations in extrapancreatic NETs are rare, though small-bowel NETs commonly show loss of chromosome 18 and CDKN1B mutations in a minority. In carcinoid syndrome the principal mediator is serotonin (5-HT), synthesized from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase; up to 50% of dietary tryptophan can be diverted into this pathway, which can deplete niacin and produce pellagra-like lesions. Histamine and tachykinins such as substance P also contribute. Serotonin stimulates intestinal secretion and motility and drives fibroblast growth, accounting for mesenteric fibrosis and for valvular fibrosis via activation of 5-HT2B receptors on heart-valve fibroblasts. Right-sided cardiac predominance reflects venous delivery of serotonin from hepatic/retroperitoneal deposits to the right heart, with pulmonary metabolism sparing the left heart. Inherited syndromes (MEN 1, von Hippel-Lindau, neurofibromatosis type 1, tuberous sclerosis) underlie a minority of cases (Harrison 22e p.676-683).
additionalDifferentials: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and other nonneuroendocrine pancreatic cancers
Irritable bowel syndrome (small-bowel NETs are frequently misattributed to IBS for months to years)
Psychiatric illness (insulinoma hypoglycemic symptoms may be mistaken for psychiatric disease)
Mixed neuroendocrine-adenocarcinoma tumors (adenocarcinoids) of the appendix
nonInfectiousMimics: Systemic mastocytosis (symptoms can be easily confused with carcinoid syndrome)
Other causes of fasting hypoglycemia: severe liver disease, alcoholism, poor nutrition, post-gastric-bypass postprandial hypoglycemia, surreptitious insulin or sulfonylurea use (mimicking insulinoma)
Causes of secretory diarrhea mimicking VIPoma: inflammatory bowel disease, short-bowel after small-bowel resection, radiation enteritis, surreptitious laxative/diuretic use
Causes of hypergastrinemia other than gastrinoma: proton pump inhibitor use and achlorhydria from chronic atrophic gastritis (mimicking gastrinoma)
Drug-induced valvulopathy mimicking carcinoid heart disease: fenfluramine and ergot-containing dopamine agonists (both act via 5-HT2B receptors)
additionalInvestigations: Somatostatin-receptor imaging: gallium-68 dotatate (or DOTATOC, copper-64 dotatate) PET, highly sensitive for primaries and metastases
Cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI; endoscopic ultrasound especially for small pancreatic primaries such as insulinomas
FDG-PET (often negative in low-grade well-differentiated NETs but positive in higher-grade tumors)
Fasting insulin with proinsulin and C-peptide (elevated in insulinoma; proinsulin/C-peptide normal with exogenous insulin) and serum/plasma sulfonylurea levels
Fasting serum gastrin (interpret with awareness of PPI and achlorhydria effects)
Plasma glucagon (glucagonoma generally >1000 pg/mL), plasma somatostatin, plasma VIP
24-hour urinary or plasma 5-HIAA for carcinoid syndrome (suggestive, not diagnostic; serotonin-rich foods such as salmon and eggs cause false positives)
Chromogranin A (neither sensitive nor specific; falsely elevated in renal impairment and with PPI use)
Histologic grading with mitotic count and Ki-67 plus chromogranin/synaptophysin immunostaining; vitamin B12 and antiparietal evaluation in type 1 gastric NET with atrophic gastritis
redFlags: Carcinoid crisis: life-threatening profound hypotension or hypertension triggered by tumor manipulation during surgery, hepatic artery embolization, radionuclide therapy, exogenous epinephrine, or anesthesia induction
Right-sided heart failure from carcinoid heart disease, a major source of morbidity and mortality
Severe refractory hypoglycemia from insulinoma causing confusion, coma
Mesenteric fibrosis causing intermittent small-bowel obstruction or bowel ischemia
Profound watery diarrhea with hypokalemia and dehydration in VIPoma (Verner-Morrison/WDHA syndrome)
harrison.prognosis: NETs are typically more indolent than other malignancies, and both incidence and survival have risen over recent decades (US incidence rose about 6.4-fold from 1973 to 2012; prevalence exceeded 170,000). Prognosis depends strongly on primary site and histologic grade. Median survival for advanced pancreatic NETs rose from roughly 2 years in early SEER analyses to about 4 years more recently, and median survival for well-differentiated advanced small-intestine NETs exceeds 5 years. Appendiceal NETs that are well differentiated and <2 cm have extremely low metastatic risk and excellent prognosis, while metastatic risk rises to about 20-30% for 2-3 cm tumors and is even higher beyond 3 cm. Most rectal NETs are small (<1 cm), well differentiated and rarely metastasize, but up to one-third of 1-2 cm rectal NETs metastasize and >2 cm rectal NETs metastasize in over 70%. Poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas carry markedly worse prognosis. The natural history is ultimately progressive (Harrison 22e p.677-682).
pitfalls: PPIs and achlorhydria can both raise serum gastrin and confound the diagnosis of gastrinoma
Chromogranin A is frequently falsely elevated (renal impairment, PPI use) and is neither sensitive nor specific; assay variability complicates interpretation
Elevated 5-HIAA is suggestive but not diagnostic of carcinoid syndrome, with false positives from serotonin-rich foods

Somatostatin-receptor PET can be falsely positive (physiologic uptake in the pancreatic uncinate process, sarcoidosis, meningiomas, thyroid goiter/thyroiditis) and falsely negative in higher-grade tumors with lower receptor expression
Insulinomas are less reliably avid on somatostatin scintigraphy and are usually small (<2 cm), making EUS the preferred localization tool
Insulinoma may be misdiagnosed as psychiatric illness; surreptitious insulin/hypoglycemic-agent use can mimic it
Small-bowel NETs are easily missed at colonoscopy due to submucosal location beyond the ileocecal valve and may be misattributed to IBS for years
Reduction of serotonin levels does not reverse established carcinoid valvular lesions
harrison.severityClassification: WHO-type histologic classification used in Harrison: well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor grade 1 (low grade, <2 mitoses/10 HPF, Ki-67 <3%); grade 2 (intermediate, 2-20/10 HPF, Ki-67 3-20%); grade 3 (well-differentiated high grade, >20/10 HPF, Ki-67 >20%); and poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma (high grade, >20/10 HPF, Ki-67 >20%), the most clinically aggressive category (Harrison 22e p.677).
management: Surgical resection is the mainstay for localised well-differentiated tumours and can be curative
Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide and lanreotide control hormonal secretory syndromes and provide an antiproliferative benefit
Manage carcinoid syndrome with somatostatin analogues, the serotonin-synthesis inhibitor telotristat for refractory diarrhoea, and niacin supplementation to prevent pellagra
Treat functional pancreatic tumours by countering their hormone, using proton-pump inhibition for gastrinoma and diazoxide for insulinoma

For advanced disease, use peptide receptor radionuclide therapy with lutetium-DOTATATE, targeted agents such as everolimus and sunitinib, and liver-directed therapy, reserving platinum-based chemotherapy with etoposide for poorly differentiated high-grade carcinomas
Surveil for carcinoid heart disease with echocardiography and monitor with chromogranin A, urinary 5-HIAA and somatostatin-receptor imaging
Manage through a neuroendocrine tumour multidisciplinary team, with genetic counselling and screening where MEN1 or another hereditary syndrome is identified
